REST, GraphQL, SOAP… choosing an API isn't just about knowing the names. It's about understanding what your system actually needs. 👇

Think about the applications you use every day:
🌦️ A weather app fetching live data
🔐 A website handling login requests
🏦 A banking platform processing transactions
📊 A dashboard retrieving data from multiple services
🤝 Two companies connecting their systems

All of these can involve APIs, but the way they communicate can be very different.
Here's a quick breakdown of the types shown in this visual:

🔹 REST APIs - Common for web apps, product data, and authentication.
🔹 SOAP APIs - Often used in enterprise environments where strict contracts and established integration standards matter.
🔹 GraphQL APIs - Useful when clients need flexibility in choosing exactly which data they want.
🔹 Internal APIs - Connect services within an application or organization, such as a frontend, backend, and database layer.
🔹 Partner APIs - Enable integrations with external businesses, payment providers, booking platforms, and other services.
🔹 Data-Sharing APIs - Allow systems to exchange information across platforms, such as logistics, finance, or healthcare data.

One important thing to remember: these categories aren't all mutually exclusive. REST, SOAP, and GraphQL describe API approaches, while internal, partner, and data-sharing APIs describe how or where APIs are used.

When designing a system, the better questions are:
→ Who will consume the API?
→ What data needs to be exchanged?
→ How should authentication and security work?
→ What performance, reliability, and compatibility requirements exist?

Understanding these trade-offs is what helps you move beyond simply using APIs to designing better backend systems.

#TheInfrastructureofFinance | The Physical Layer
The people on the night shift

Most of what I write here can be measured in megawatts, square feet or dollars per megawatt. Today's subject doesn't appear on any spec sheet. It's the people who keep the physical layer running at three in the morning on a holiday weekend, when the utility blinks and the generators have about ten seconds to prove they were worth buying. I learned this early in my first job on raised floor as a night-shift tape librarian. I sat in front of an IBM 3278 terminal watching UCC-1 pop up a tape number and a drive number. I would then run down the endless aisle of hanging 9-track tapes, get the right one, put it on the right drive, make sure it mounted, and then run back for the next one. (Anyone else on here remember UCC-1?)

Every bank's resilience plan ends up in a building, and every building ends up depending on a shift engineer with a flashlight, a procedure and the judgment to know when the procedure doesn't quite fit. Uptime Institute's outage research makes the point better than I can. In its 2025 report, nearly 40% of organizations said they'd had a major outage caused by human error in the previous three years, and 85% of those came from staff not following procedures (most of the rest came from the procedures themselves). This year's report says failure to follow procedures is still the leading cause of human-error outages. I don't take that to mean people are the weak link. I take it to mean that training, drills and a culture where a technician feels free to stop and ask are as much a part of the infrastructure as the switchgear.

The trouble is there aren't enough of them. Uptime's 2025 staffing survey of 864 operators found that hiring qualified people is still a top worry, and that junior facilities staff are in the shortest supply and leave the fastest, especially at colocation providers. Meanwhile the industry is building at a pace I haven't seen in thirty-plus years, and the new liquid-cooled #AI ask more of the people who run them. Plumbing, it turns out, is back.

The industry is settling on the old answer, which is to grow your own. In the UK and Ireland, Digital Realty has been building its own apprentice programmes, including an electrical craft apprenticeship launched in Ireland this spring with CJK Academy, and the two cohorts recently got together in London to compare notes. It's slow, unglamorous work, and it never makes the press release about the next hundred megawatts.

For those of us in financial services, this comes down to a practical question. When you review a provider's resilience, you ask about the generators, the fuel contracts and the cooling redundancy. Ask about the people too: how many are on site overnight, how they're trained, how often they drill, and how long they stay.

If you'd like to meet some of them, and see what a well-run night shift looks like, let me know. I'll bring the coffee and donuts. They've earned it.

Completed your AI interview but haven't received any feedback? Here's what you should know. 👇

Many candidates assume that if they haven't heard back after an AI interview, something went wrong. But that's not necessarily the case.
Let's look at what might be happening and what you can do to improve your chances of getting hired. I'll use Micro1 - > https://lnkd.in/dSMRnUmf  as an example, but similar principles apply to other AI talent platforms.

🔹 1. Why haven't you received feedback?
There are several possible explanations:

1.1 You didn't pass the interview. In this case, you'll likely receive an email, although it may take some time. The timeline depends on the position and how actively the hiring team is recruiting.
1.2. Your interview is still under review. You may have performed well, but your results still need to be reviewed by a human evaluator.
1.3. The position may already be filled. Even if you passed the interview, the hiring team might already have enough qualified candidates.

This is particularly relevant for older job postings. Based on what I've observed, your chances are significantly better when you apply within the first 24–48 hours.

🔹 2. Why a successful interview is valuable, even without a job offer
Here's something many candidates don't realize.

When you successfully complete an interview and receive certification, you can earn Vetted Skills that become part of your talent profile.
These skills remain associated with your account and can help you qualify for future opportunities.
As you build more Vetted Skills, you may be able to apply for certain positions without repeating the entire interview process. In some cases, you may only need to complete a partial interview.
This means that even if your interview didn't lead to a project, it may still have strengthened your profile for future applications.

🔹 3. What should you do next?
Rather than waiting for a response to one application, I recommend focusing on three things:
✅ Apply to fresh positions. Ideally, look for roles published within the last 24–48 hours, when hiring is most active.
✅ Choose roles that match your experience. The closer your skills are to the requirements, the better your chances.
✅ Continue building your Vetted Skills. Each successful interview can make your profile more competitive and potentially simplify future applications.
The important thing to understand is that certification and project placement are two separate steps.
You can successfully pass an interview without receiving an offer for that particular position. But your certification may still be useful when you apply for the next one.
So if you've completed your AI interview and haven't heard back, don't assume you've reached a dead end.
Keep applying to relevant opportunities, prioritize fresh openings, and use each successful interview to strengthen your profile.

I've really enjoyed competing with both Seismic and Highspot over the years. Good competition makes all companies stronger, and I always welcome it.

But now that they’re one company (Heismic, as we call it), a lot of things will change. 

They brought two businesses together to be more profitable. Both companies raised a lot of capital, and their investors have high expectations.

There were massive layoffs in the first week after the merger officially closed.

This was inevitable, I just didn't think it would happen this fast. 

First, I always come to the people. I think the Highspot team has been impacted the most so far in the first round, and that's hard to see. 

These are good people, and some of them have already joined Allego. Our thoughts are with the rest of them who are now searching for a new job.

The second wave of impact always hits the customers.

Since the merger officially closed, countless companies have reached out to us and said:
"I lost my account manager."
"I lost my customer success manager."
"I'm nervous about what's next."
"How are they going to bring two products together?" 

The truth is you can't run two separate platforms under one company.

Analyst firms have summed it up best when they characterized the Seismic-Highspot transaction as a defensive consolidation designed to address pricing pressures, CRM market overlap, and emerging AI threats. 

These analysts have advised their customers on either platform to limit renewals to one year to mitigate integration risks and preserve negotiating leverage.

Our challenge as a brand has always been awareness. We haven't had the same marketing budgets as our competitors. Instead, we’ve spent our money developing our product and our people.

This is our opportunity to show a whole new segment who Allego is and how we can help them be successful.

We're hiring across nearly every team at Allego, so if the layoffs have impacted you, reach out, and I'll connect you with the right person on our team.                                                                                                                                                          
And if you're an unhappy customer on either platform, we have a contract buyout program that gives you free access to our platform today. Send me a message, and I'll send over all the details.

You don’t buy AI. You put it on the payroll. And right now, most businesses are accidentally paying CEO wages for data-entry work.

I remember when scaling a team meant signing a $40,000 annual SaaS contract just to add 30 more user seats. It did not matter if your staff used the software ten hours a day or ten minutes a month. The vendor got their flat fee.

AI completely blew that model up. Now, you pay by the token. Pure variable pricing.

In theory, it is amazing. A small business can process 10,000 customer support tickets for maybe $40 in API costs instead of hiring three more reps. You only pay for the exact compute you consume.

But here is the ugly side of variable pricing. It has absolutely no ceiling.

I have seen businesses plug a top-tier model into their operations and wake up to a $2,800 OpenAI bill a week later. Why? Because they set it up poorly. The AI was forced to read an entire 50-message email history, including all the legal footers and signatures, just to answer a customer asking Do you ship to Ohio?

Every word fed into the system costs a fraction of a cent. When you run an inefficient loop a thousand times a day, it bleeds your cash.

This problem is getting so expensive that an entire sector of startups is being built right now just to fix it. They do one thing: intelligent model routing.

Think of them like a dispatcher. When a prompt comes in, the router looks at it and decides how much actual brainpower the task needs.

If the task is just extracting a phone number from a document, the router hands it to a tiny, ultra-cheap model. It costs you $0.0001. But if the prompt requires complex logic or heavy reasoning, it gets bumped up to a flagship model.

The user on the other end gets the exact same quality of answer. But the business cuts its total token spend by 80%.

You do not even need to buy a router to do this. You just have to build your systems with a little bit of financial discipline.

First, stop using AI for things traditional code can do for free. If a basic Zapier rule can tag an email based on the subject line, let the code do it. Save your paid tokens for actual thinking.

Second, put your context on a diet. You pay for what the AI reads. Strip out the junk data, the disclaimers, and the blank spaces before you send the prompt over.

Massive scale no longer requires a massive upfront software budget. It just requires you to manage the meter.

What has stopped you from plugging AI into your business so far?

This framework works.

⚬ My troops at Vets Who Code are using it to land interviews right now.

The session is going to be highly data-intensive and heavily AI-focused. You’ll walk away with the exact artifacts, resources, and actionable strategies you need to beat the automated screening systems and stand out to hiring managers.

“How much does HR software cost per employee?” is the first question most buyers ask, and the least useful one to answer with a single number.

Two quotes can both say “per employee” and still describe completely different purchases. One counts only active staff, the other counts everyone with a record. One includes onboarding and time-off, the other adds reviews and a service desk as extras. One has a platform fee, an implementation charge, a minimum commitment. The other doesn’t mention them until the contract.

So the number worth comparing isn’t the headline rate. It’s the complete recurring bill divided by the employees it actually covers. Here is how to get there:

1. Ask who counts as a billable employee.
 Active staff, contractors, people on leave, people who have left but whose records remain. Get the definition in writing and apply it to every quote on your shortlist.

2. Match the scope.
 List the work you need the software to support on day one, and separately what you may add later. Then ask each vendor to quote the same scope.

3. Add up the recurring charges.
 Employee subscription, selected modules, any platform fee. Divide by the employees covered, for the same billing period.

4. Keep one-time costs separate.
 Implementation, migration and configuration belong in the first-year budget, not in the monthly rate. Otherwise you can’t tell what you’ll pay next year.

5. Ask what happens when headcount changes.
 When does billing adjust, and does a minimum commitment apply? If you’re hiring, ask for the same configuration at the size you’re planning for, not just today’s.

6. Send every vendor the same brief.
 Workforce categories, launch workflows, later workflows, the systems you’re keeping, who owns implementation. A narrow quote shouldn’t look cheaper only because it leaves out what another includes.

And keep two documents: a cost comparison, and a checklist of whether the proposed scope handles your real processes. A clear quote with no demonstrated workflow is half a decision, and so is a great demo with vague contract terms.

This is where HRSpace makes it easier. It’s a modular cloud platform with per-employee pricing, covering onboarding, time-off, performance reviews, goals, recognition, AI recruitment and an internal service desk. That means you decide which functions go into the first quote and which wait. Platform scope doesn’t tell you your package, so confirm the included modules, the billable employee definition and implementation responsibilities in your own proposal.

You hired AI.

Then locked it out of the records room.

Across many SAP environments, the intelligence needed by AI already exists.

It is sitting inside:

• Invoices
• Contracts
• Engineering drawings
• Purchase orders
• Maintenance records
• Vendor correspondence

The problem is not a lack of data.

The problem is that decades of business evidence remain trapped inside fragmented repositories, expensive legacy ECM platforms and proprietary content architectures.

So organizations invest in copilots, agents and large language models, then give them access to only a fraction of the business context.

That is like hiring the world’s best investigator and refusing to hand over the case files.

A better approach is practical:

SAP retains the transaction and business context.

Your Azure, AWS or Google Cloud environment controls the content.

IntelliDocX preserves the links, permissions, retention and governance that connect them.

You do not need another enormous transformation program.

Start with one content-heavy process, make its evidence accessible to AI and measure the outcome.

Before buying another AI tool, ask one question:

Can our AI actually read the documents where our business knowledge lives?

My Experience at Collective Artists Network (Galleri5)

I recently got laid off from Collective Artists Networks Galleri5 division, just five months into my one-year contract. But what disappointed me wasnt just the layoff. It was everything that happened before it. I joined on April 13 as an AI + 3D Generalist.
 During hiring, HR mentioned multiple upcoming projects, possible contract extensions, and working hours of Monday–Friday, 10 AM–6:30 PM, with Saturdays as WFH if required.

On my very first day, I learned that Saturdays werent off. Initially, I was assigned to Krishna, while another team worked on Hanuman. Some newly hired artists remained unassigned for weeks, and a few were terminated before even starting project work so why were they even hired. In June, our entire Krishna team was shifted to Hanuman due to production deadlines, yet some unassigned artists still werent included and were eventually laid off. Why hire artists if there isnt enough work for them, especially when another team is overloaded? We worked 10–12+ hours daily, Monday through Saturday, with Sunday work also expected, without additional monetary compensation for my extra hours. Instead, we were promised two weeks of compensatory leave.Despite repeated layoffs creating constant job insecurity, we continued giving our best to the project. By mid-August, the films first pass was completed. I scheduled my promised leave for September 7–18. Before leaving, a team lead even offered me another project after my return.But during that very leave, HR called to inform me I was being terminated due to downsizing. HR initially asked me to resign voluntarily, which I refused since the decision wasnt mine. I received my termination letter on September 16.When I returned my laptop, the team lead told me he hadnt known about my termination and had requested management to retain me for his project, but the decision was already processed.If another team needed my skills, why wasnt that considered before terminating me?

Even my full-and-final settlement arrived on October 8, later than the seven-working-day timeline communicated by HR.

I understand my contract allowed early termination, and downsizing sometimes happens. But recruitment promises that dont match reality, poor resource management, excessive working hours, and constant job insecurity shouldnt be normalized.Artists are expected to treat projects as their own, sacrifice weekends, and give everything to meet deadlines. But once the work is completed, are those same artists simply an expense to be cut?Im sharing my experience because artists deserve transparency, fair working conditions, and respect.

Before approving another headcount request, I would ask five questions.

When a business unit asks for 20 new hires, 9 out of 10 times they don't have a hiring problem. They have a #workforceplanningproblem.

#Hiring is the most expensive reflex to a capacity crunch. As #HR leaders navigating AI adoption and shifting skill demands, our job isn't to fill seats it's to architect capability.

Before posting a single JD, run this filter:
#CriticalRole RealityCheck: Does this deliver core competitive advantage, or is it operational drift?

#DemandForecastStressTest: Is this volume spike durable for 18 months, or a 90-day seasonal backlog?

#ProductivityBaseline: Have we integrated GenAI and streamlined broken handoffs, or are we just throwing headcount at bad process design?

#SkillsInventory: What adjacent talent already sits inside our teams, ready for a 6-week reskill or internal move?

#Build vs. #BuyEconomics: Can we contract the peak, automate the workflow, and build the critical core internally?

Growth doesn't come from aggressive hiring. It comes from disciplined workforce allocation.

What’s the first question you ask before signing off on headcount?

My story of 4 jobs landed without email, AI, LinkedIn OR responding to postings (back then it was ads in the paper) . . . in both strong and rough job markets. 

JOB #1: 

I spoke with friends who landed roles and was pointed to a temp-to-perm agency, where I landed a permanent role at an Association in Washington, DC.

TAKEAWAY LESSON: Consider contract or fractional roles. 

JOB #2: 

I told friends I was unhappy with Job #1, and my friend at the World Bank told me about a small consulting firm she worked with that was hiring . After reaching out with her referral and getting an interview, I was hired. 

TAKEAWAY LESSON: Don't overlook small companies or boutique firms. 

JOB #3: 

With plans to relocate and make a career pivot after earning my master's in a graduate social work program, I reached out to current and former professors and asked if they knew any colleagues in my new city. One did. 

I left a voicemail asking if we could speak, which we did. She gave me a few names, and I rinsed and repeated to land a role doing social work case management for a Medicaid home health hospice program. 

TAKEAWAY LESSON: Tap into warm but second-string contacts in your network. 

JOB #4: 

I told anyone I came in contact with that I was looking to pivot AGAIN (this time back to corporate from social work). I shared with them what I was good at (writing and listening to people) and the type of role I was targeting.

An alum a few years ahead of me introduced me to a recruiter at a growing financial services company. He said I'd be great for a newly created and as-yet-unpublished role managing a small Communications and Training team at one of their de novo startups. 

I went through a series of interviews and an assessment before I was offered and accepted the role.

TAKEAWAY LESSON: The more targeted the ask, the greater the help.

REST, GraphQL, SOAP… choosing an API isn't just about knowing the names. It's about understanding what your system actually needs. 👇

Think about the applications you use every day:
🌦️ A weather app fetching live data
🔐 A website handling login requests
🏦 A banking platform processing transactions
📊 A dashboard retrieving data from multiple services
🤝 Two companies connecting their systems

All of these can involve APIs, but the way they communicate can be very different.
Here's a quick breakdown of the types shown in this visual:
🔹 REST APIs - Common for web apps, product data, and authentication.
🔹 SOAP APIs - Often used in enterprise environments where strict contracts and established integration standards matter.
🔹 GraphQL APIs - Useful when clients need flexibility in choosing exactly which data they want.
🔹 Internal APIs - Connect services within an application or organization, such as a frontend, backend, and database layer.
🔹 Partner APIs - Enable integrations with external businesses, payment providers, booking platforms, and other services.
🔹 Data-Sharing APIs - Allow systems to exchange information across platforms, such as logistics, finance, or healthcare data.

One important thing to remember: these categories aren't all mutually exclusive. REST, SOAP, and GraphQL describe API approaches, while internal, partner, and data-sharing APIs describe how or where APIs are used.

When designing a system, the better questions are:
→ Who will consume the API?
→ What data needs to be exchanged?
→ How should authentication and security work?
→ What performance, reliability, and compatibility requirements exist?
Understanding these trade-offs is what helps you move beyond simply using APIs to designing better backend systems.
